literal: He Ba, Xi Mu, Mo Ti, Yu Yeyan, He Digan, Li Li, Liu Jie, Gu Bi, Zhang Li
idiomatic: He Ba, Xi Mu, Mo Ti, Yu Yeyan, He Digan, Li Li, Liu Jie, Gu Bi, and Zhang Li

literal: He Ba was a man of Dai; for generations his clan had led the tribe and served as an attached subject of the state.
idiomatic: He Ba came from Dai. His line had led their tribe for generations as vassals of the Wei.

literal: Ba was famed for talent in debate; Taizu raised him to outer-court grandee, had him take part in the state's great counsels, and he was by nature skilled in stratagem.
idiomatic: Ba won renown for eloquence and wit. Taizu made him an outer-court grandee and drew him into the realm's weightiest counsels; he had a gift for calculation and design.

literal: On repeated missions he hit the mark of the ruler's intent and was appointed General of Dragon Agility.
idiomatic: Mission after mission pleased the throne, and he was named General of Dragon Agility.

literal: Before long he was granted the title Duke of Rinan.
idiomatic: Soon after he received the title Duke of Rinan.

literal: He followed in pacifying the Central Plains; for merit he was advanced to Master of Writing and stationed to guard Ye.
idiomatic: He marched in the pacification of the Central Plains and, for his service, was promoted to Master of Writing and set to guard Ye.

literal: Murong De sent his elder brother's son He to hold Huatai; He's chief clerk Li Bian killed He and sought aid from Ba.
idiomatic: Murong De had his brother's son He defend Huatai. He's chief clerk, Li Bian, murdered him and appealed to Ba for rescue.

literal: Ba led light cavalry to hurry there.
idiomatic: Ba rode at the head of light cavalry to answer the call.

literal: When he had arrived, Bian repented and shut the gates to refuse and defend.
idiomatic: Once Ba arrived, Bian regretted his move, barred the gates, and held the city against him.

literal: Ba sent Masters of Writing gentleman Deng Hui to persuade him, and Bian then opened the gates.
idiomatic: Ba sent Deng Hui of the Masters of Writing to reason with him, and Bian at last opened the gates.

literal: Ba entered and seized the treasury stores.
idiomatic: Ba entered the city and took possession of the treasury.

literal: De heard of it and sent a general leading three thousand horsemen to strike Ba.
idiomatic: When De learned of it, he dispatched a general with three thousand horsemen to attack Ba.

literal: Ba met the attack head-on, routed them utterly, and returned having captured more than a thousand of their officers and soldiers.
idiomatic: Ba met them head-on and broke their force, then withdrew with more than a thousand captives among officers and men.

literal: Thereupon many of the people of Chen and Ying came to submit and be transformed.
idiomatic: After that, multitudes from Chen and Ying turned toward Wei rule.

literal: His fief was changed to Duke of Dingling.
idiomatic: His title was changed to Duke of Dingling.

literal: With the Prince of Changshan, Zun, he led fifty thousand men to campaign against Muyi Yu, a separate chieftain of the Helan tribe, and defeated him.
idiomatic: He and the Prince of Changshan, Zun, took fifty thousand men against Muyi Yu, a splinter chief of the Helan, and crushed him.

literal: He went out and became Grand Warden of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: He was sent out to serve as grand warden of Pingyuan.

literal: Taizu favored and met with Ba; among the generals he stood at the crown.
idiomatic: Taizu showered favor on Ba above every other commander.

literal: At the time the ministers all honored and prized respectful frugality, yet Ba loved to cultivate empty reputation and dazzle the age; his nature was especially extravagant and dissolute. Taizu admonished him, but he did not reform.
idiomatic: While the court cultivated sober humility, Ba courted hollow glory and flaunted his splendor before the age. He was by nature given to excess. Taizu warned him, yet he would not mend his ways.

literal: Later, when the imperial carriage hunted north at Jackal Mountain, Ba was seized and executed by the roadside.
idiomatic: Later, during a northern hunt at Jackal Mountain, the emperor had Ba seized and put to death beside the road.

literal: His wife, Lady Liu, killed herself to follow him.
idiomatic: His wife, Lady Liu, took her own life to follow him in death.

literal: Earlier, when Ba was about to be executed, Taizu ordered his younger brothers Pi and the rest to witness the farewell; Ba told Pi: "The land north of Zei is poor soil—you may dwell south of the waters, take up cultivation on rich fields, broaden your estates, each urge the other on, and strive to build yourselves up.
idiomatic: Before the execution Taizu had Ba's brothers, Pi among them, come for a final parting. Ba told Pi, "The country north of Zei is thin. Settle south of the river, farm the good land, build your holdings wide, and press one another to better your houses.

literal: " He then turned his back on them and said: "How can you bear to watch me die!"
idiomatic: Then he turned from them and cried, "How can you stand by and watch me die!"

literal: Pi and the others grasped his subtle intent; they falsely claimed to be envoys, saying they were fleeing to Chang'an, and pursued him but could not overtake.
idiomatic: Pi and his brothers caught his hidden meaning. They pretended to be messengers bound for Chang'an and gave chase, but could not catch up.

literal: Taizu was enraged and thereupon executed the whole family.
idiomatic: Taizu flew into rage and put the entire house to the sword.

literal: Later Shizu on a western tour to Wuyuan turned back to hunt at Jackal Mountain, when suddenly a violent wind arose and clouds and mist closed in on every side.
idiomatic: Later, Shizu toured the west as far as Wuyuan, then returned to hunt at Jackal Mountain. A sudden gale rose; cloud and mist walled the sky on every hand.

literal: Shizu found it strange and questioned them; the assembled ministers all said that Ba for generations had dwelt on this soil, that his shrine tomb still stood, and that perhaps he could bring about such a change.
idiomatic: Shizu marveled and asked what it meant. The court together declared that Ba's line had long held this land, that his ancestral shrine still stood, and that he might have stirred this omen.

literal: The emperor sent Gu Bi, Duke of Jianxing, to offer sacrifice with the three sacrificial beasts; the mist at once dispersed.
idiomatic: The emperor sent Gu Bi, Duke of Jianxing, to sacrifice with the triple offering of ox, sheep, and pig. The fog lifted at once.

literal: Afterward, on days when Shizu went hunting, he always sacrificed to Ba first.
idiomatic: From then on, whenever Shizu took the field on a hunt, he made offering to Ba before all else.

literal: His youngest son Gui, in campaigning against Helian Chang with merit, was appointed General of Tongwan and granted the title Baron of Chenggao.
idiomatic: His youngest son Gui earned merit against Helian Chang, was made General of Tongwan, and enfeoffed as Baron of Chenggao.

literal: With the Prince of Xiping, Anji, he attacked Hulao and took it.
idiomatic: With the Prince of Xiping, Anji, he stormed Hulao and captured it.

literal: His rank was advanced to Marquis of Gaoyang.
idiomatic: He was raised to Marquis of Gaoyang.

literal: Later, for a crime he was banished and assigned to Liang Province as a commoner.
idiomatic: Later, condemned for a crime, he was exiled to common status in Liang Province.

literal: When Gai Wu rebelled in Guanzhong, Gui was again appointed Dragon Agile General and sent to campaign against him.
idiomatic: When Gai Wu rose in revolt in Guanzhong, Gui was again named Dragon Agile General and sent to suppress him.

literal: On his return he was appointed Bearer of the Staff of Authority, Champion General, Grand Commander of the Garrison at Yongcheng, and Marquis of Gaoyang.
idiomatic: On his return he received the staff of authority as champion general, grand commander of the Yongcheng garrison, and Marquis of Gaoyang.

literal: He came to his end.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Du inherited the title.
idiomatic: His son Du succeeded to the title.

literal: Gentleman of the Masters of Writing, Bureau of Punishments, and Grand Warden of Changping.
idiomatic: He served as gentleman in the Masters of Writing, bureau of punishments, and as grand warden of Changping.

literal: He expired.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: Du's son Yanmu was a clerk in the commandery offices of Si Province and died young.
idiomatic: Du's son Yanmu held a clerkship in the Si Province commanderies and died in his prime.

literal: His son An, at the end of the Wuding era, was Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: His son An, in the last years of Wuding, served as attendant gentleman of the yellow gate.

literal: Xi Mu was a man of Dai, grave and steady, with wisdom and stratagem.
idiomatic: Xi Mu came from Dai—steady, weighty in counsel, and shrewd in design.

literal: Taizu favored and met with him and called him his second elder brother.
idiomatic: Taizu favored him warmly and addressed him as a second elder brother.

literal: Earlier, when Liu Xian plotted to harm Taizu, Liang Juan learned of the plot and secretly sent Mu with Mu Chong to Qijie Mountain to report it—the account is in Chong's biography.
idiomatic: When Liu Xian once plotted against Taizu's life, Liang Juan uncovered the scheme and secretly sent Mu with Mu Chong to Qijie Mountain to warn him—the full tale stands in Chong's biography.

literal: Taizu recorded the old ministers of the former emperor, and because Mu had reported Xian's plot he was appointed Chief Who Governs the People, presented and played out government affairs, and took part in planning.
idiomatic: Taizu honored the veterans of the former reign and, for Mu's warning against Xian, made him chief who governs the people, set him to frame and present policy, and drew him into counsel.

literal: When Taizu campaigned against Murong Bao he was added as General Who Supports the State; he overran the Jin region and at Pingtao captured Bao's Prince of Danyang, Maid, and the Protector of the Army of Lishi, Gao Xiuhe.
idiomatic: On Taizu's campaign against Murong Bao, Mu was named general who supports the state. He swept the Jin territories and at Pingtao took Bao's Prince of Danyang, Maid, together with Gao Xiuhe, protector of the army at Lishi.

literal: For military merit he was appointed Regional Inspector of Bing and granted the title Duke of Rencheng.
idiomatic: For his victories he was made regional inspector of Bing and enfeoffed Duke of Rencheng.

literal: The province bordered Yao Xing's domain; Xing often raided the frontier. Mu then wrote to Xing, styling himself with forehead to ground and using the balanced epistolary form to resist him, reproaching Xing for the injustice of invading the border.
idiomatic: Bing shared a border with Yao Xing, who raided often. Mu wrote to him in the full forms of submission—forehead to earth, balanced courtesy—yet turned the letter into a rebuke of Xing's border raids as unjust.

literal: Xing, because the state was in communication and alliance, hated this.
idiomatic: Xing, bound to Wei by treaty, took the letter as an outrage.

literal: Someone spoke of it to Taizu, and Taizu executed him.
idiomatic: Word reached Taizu, and he had Mu put to death.

literal: Mo Ti was a man of Dai, of much wisdom and with talent for use.
idiomatic: Mo Ti came from Dai—clever, resourceful, and fit for command.

literal: At first he was a standard-bearer general and led the forbidden troops.
idiomatic: He first served as standard-bearer general in charge of the palace guard.

literal: When Taizu campaigned against Murong Bao, Bao came by night to attack the camp and the chariot soldiers were thrown into terror.
idiomatic: During Taizu's campaign against Murong Bao, Bao struck the camp by night and the army fell into panic.

literal: Thereupon some fled back to the capital, saying the government army had been defeated at Baixi; the capital was unsettled.
idiomatic: Runners carried word to the capital that the imperial army had been broken at Baixi, and the city trembled with fear.

literal: The Prince of Nan'an, Yuan Shun, took advantage of this and wished to seize control of state affairs.
idiomatic: The Prince of Nan'an, Yuan Shun, seized on the alarm and moved to take the reins of government.

literal: Ti said to Shun: "This is a great matter and cannot be treated lightly; you should carefully await later developments—otherwise disaster will reach you.
idiomatic: Ti told Shun, "This is no small matter. Do not act rashly. Wait until the truth is clear—otherwise ruin will find you.

literal: " Shun then stopped.
idiomatic: Shun held back.

literal: For merit he was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distance, granted the title Duke of Foliu, advanced in title to Left General, and changed to Duke of Gaoyi.
idiomatic: For his service he was named general who pacifies the distance, enfeoffed Duke of Foliu, raised to left general, and then made Duke of Gaoyi.

literal: He went out and was removed to Grand Warden of Zhongshan, supervising the seven commanderies east of the mountains in Si Province.
idiomatic: He was sent out as grand warden of Zhongshan, with oversight of the seven eastern commanderies of Si Province beyond the Taihang.

literal: When the imperial carriage campaigned against Yao Xing it halted at Jinyang; bandits of Shangdang—Qin Po of the masses and Zhai Du of the Dingling—gathered their followers at Huguan. An edict ordered Ti to command three thousand men to campaign against them.
idiomatic: While the emperor campaigned against Yao Xing and paused at Jinyang, brigands of Shangdang—Qin Po among the people and the Dingling leader Zhai Du—raised bands at Huguan. Ti was ordered to take three thousand men against them.

literal: The Grand Warden of Shangdang captured Po and beheaded him.
idiomatic: The grand warden of Shangdang seized Po and struck off his head.

literal: Du fled to Linlu.
idiomatic: Du fled into the hills at Linlu.

literal: An edict ordered Ti to search the mountains and pursue to the end, and he pacified them completely.
idiomatic: Ti was commanded to comb the mountains and hunt them down to the last man until the region was quiet.

literal: In the last years of Zhaocheng, Taizu's younger paternal uncle Kudou was moved to Chang'an.
idiomatic: Late in the reign of Emperor Zhaocheng, Taizu's uncle Kudou was resettled in Chang'an.

literal: When Fu Jian was defeated, he followed Murong Yong east in migration.
idiomatic: After Fu Jian's fall he marched east with Murong Yong.

literal: When Yong declared himself ruler, he made Kudou Grand Warden of Xinxing.
idiomatic: When Yong took the throne, he appointed Kudou grand warden of Xinxing.

literal: At the opening of Dengguo, Liu Xian sent his younger brother Kanghou and others to welcome Kudou, and they raided the southern marches.
idiomatic: In the first year of Dengguo, Liu Xian sent his brother Kanghou and others to bring Kudou home, and they harried the southern frontier.

literal: At the time Ti was disloyal to Taizu; he sent an arrow to Kudou, telling him, "Can a three-year-old calf bear a heavy load?"—meaning Kudou was elder and Taizu young.
idiomatic: Ti then stood against Taizu and sent Kudou an arrow with the message, "Can a calf of three years bear a heavy load?"—telling him the uncle was the elder strength and the nephew still a boy.

literal: Taizu thereafter harbored resentment against him.
idiomatic: Taizu never forgave the insult.

literal: In the fifth year of Tianci, someone reported that Ti in his dwelling was haughty and arrogant, taking the demeanor of a sovereign.
idiomatic: In the fifth year of Tianci, an informer accused Ti of living in insolent state, matching his manner to a ruler's.

literal: Taizu then had someone show him the arrow and tell him: "A three-year-old calf—can it bear a heavy load or not?"
idiomatic: Taizu had the arrow brought before him and asked, "A calf of three years—can it bear a heavy load?"

literal: Ti received the edict; father and son faced each other weeping, and on the morrow he was executed.
idiomatic: Ti took the decree. He and his son wept face to face through the night. At dawn they led him to execution.

literal: Yu Yeyan was a man of Dai; later he was granted the name Yue.
idiomatic: Yu Yeyan came from Dai and was later granted the personal name Yue.

literal: His father and his elder brother He Chen for generations managed the royal herds.
idiomatic: His father and elder brother He Chen had for generations overseen the imperial herds.

literal: He was gradually transferred to grandee of the central tribes.
idiomatic: He rose by degrees to grandee of the central tribes.

literal: When Zhaocheng passed away, the Di raided within the borders.
idiomatic: When Emperor Zhaocheng died, Di forces raided across the frontier.

literal: Amid the troubles he gathered in livestock and wealth until his riches rivaled the ruler's.
idiomatic: In the turmoil he rounded up herds and stores until his wealth rivaled the throne's own.

literal: When Liu Xian plotted rebellion, Taizu went out on campaign; He Chen presented Empress Dowager Ming to Taizu and also supplied him with resources.
idiomatic: When Liu Xian plotted treason and Taizu marched abroad, He Chen escorted Empress Dowager Ming back to him and furnished the army with supplies.

literal: He Chen was made Chief of the Inner Attendants.
idiomatic: He Chen was appointed chief of the inner attendants.

literal: He Chen divided the old herds of public and private stock and largely missed the mark of the ruler's intent; Taizu therefore resented him.
idiomatic: He Chen's division of the old herds between public and private stock missed Taizu's intent, and the emperor came to hate him for it.

literal: Yue alone was respectful, cautious, and strict in conduct, skilled at handling intervals of peril; Taizu delighted in him.
idiomatic: Yue alone was reverent, careful, and steady in crisis. Taizu took pleasure in him.

literal: With Wang Jian and others he was alike made outer-court grandee and took part in army and state.
idiomatic: He stood with Wang Jian and others among the outer-court grandees, sharing in military and civil counsel.

literal: When Taizu had broken with Murong Chui, he made Yue a grandee and sent him to Murong Yong.
idiomatic: After Taizu broke with Murong Chui, he named Yue a grandee and dispatched him to Murong Yong.

literal: Yong was convinced by his rhetoric and meaning.
idiomatic: Yong was won over by his words.

literal: When Chui besieged Yong at Changzi, Yong reported urgency and sought aid; Yue with the Prince of Chenliu, Qian, led fifty thousand horsemen east across the river to rescue him, halted at Xiurong, defeated the mountain Hu chieftain Gaochemen of the Gaoche tribe and others, and moved their tribes.
idiomatic: Chui besieged Yong at Changzi; Yong cried for help. Yue and the Prince of Chenliu, Qian, crossed the Yellow River at the head of fifty thousand horse, camped at Xiurong, broke the mountain Hu under the Gaoche chieftain Gaochemen, and resettled their clans.

literal: When Yong perished they withdrew the army.
idiomatic: When Yong fell, they marched home.

literal: He followed in pacifying the Central Plains and was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distance.
idiomatic: He took part in pacifying the Central Plains and was named general who pacifies the distance.

literal: When the government army was thrown into alarm at Baixi, the Helan chieftain Fuli Juan, the Getunlin chieftain Niwuni, and the Hexi chieftain Chinugen and others heard of it and gathered their factions to rebel at Yinguan.
idiomatic: When panic spread from the rout at Baixi, Fuli Juan of the Helan, Niwuni of the Getunlin, and Chinugen of the Hexi heard the news and raised their clans in revolt at Yinguan.

literal: The Prince of Nan'an, Yuan Shun, campaigned against them but could not overcome them; those who died numbered several thousand.
idiomatic: The Prince of Nan'an, Yuan Shun, marched against them and failed; thousands fell.

literal: Taizu heard of it and ordered Yue to lead ten thousand horsemen back to campaign against Chinugen and the rest, exterminating them; the common people then were at peace.
idiomatic: Taizu sent Yue back at the head of ten thousand horse to crush Chinugen and his allies. The land grew calm again.

literal: The Hu chieftain of Lishi, Huyan Tie, and the Hu chieftain of Xihe, Zhang Chong, were unwilling to move within the borders; they gathered factions and rebelled.
idiomatic: Huyan Tie, Hu chief of Lishi, and Zhang Chong of Xihe refused resettlement inland and rose with their bands.

literal: Yue led three thousand horsemen, campaigned and defeated them, beheaded Tie and captured Chong, searched the mountains and pursued to the end, and scattered the remainder of the faction.
idiomatic: Yue took three thousand horse, broke their force, slew Tie and took Chong alive, combed the hills until no rebel remained, and broke up the rest of the band.

literal: For merit he was granted the title Duke of Xichang and advanced in title to General Who Subdues the Barbarians.
idiomatic: For these victories he was enfeoffed Duke of Xichang and promoted to general who subdues the barbarians.

literal: He again campaigned against the rebel Zhang Chao and the Grand Warden of Qinghe, Fu Shi, and defeated and pacified them both.
idiomatic: He marched again against the rebel Zhang Chao and Fu Shi, grand warden of Qinghe, and brought both campaigns to ruin.

literal: Yue was made Mobile Court Commissioner at Ye.
idiomatic: Yue was appointed mobile court commissioner at Ye.

literal: As a general he had stratagem; in governing the army he was clear and orderly; he constantly used the few to strike the many; officers and soldiers submitted to his wisdom and courage—his name stood at the crown among the generals.
idiomatic: In command he was a strategist; his camps were disciplined and clean. He made a habit of beating larger forces with smaller ones. The ranks bowed to his wit and daring, and among generals his name stood first.

literal: When the mobile court at Ye was abolished, the six commanderies he had governed were set up as Xiang Province, and he was at once appointed its regional inspector.
idiomatic: When the Ye mobile court was dissolved, his six commanderies became Xiang Province, and he was immediately made its inspector.

literal: He was fair, incorrupt, and even-handed; the common people praised him.
idiomatic: He ruled with fairness and clean hands, and the people spoke well of him.

literal: Of old there were gardens and ponds; when the season's fruit first ripened, clerks and officials sent some; Yue would not accept them, saying: "The fruit has not yet been presented to the throne—how may I eat first?"
idiomatic: He kept the old gardens and orchards. When the first fruit of the season ripened, his clerks brought him a basket. Yue refused it, saying, "Until fruit reaches the imperial table, how should I taste it first?"

literal: His scrupulousness was of this sort.
idiomatic: Such was the strictness of his conduct.
